name: Catch competitors bidding on your brand terms with Bright Data, GPT-5.6, Google Sheets and Slack

parameters.content:
## See who is buying ads against your brand name

A competitor bidding on your brand takes clicks you already paid to earn, and nothing in your own analytics names them. This sweeps the paid block on your terms every morning.

### How it works

**`Build The Query Grid`** crosses your brand with the modifiers people search - `alternative`, `pricing`, `vs`, `login` - across your markets, and a **Bright Data SERP** request runs each one. Every market names a city, because the ad auction is geographic: four brand queries returned 2 ads on a country code and 12 with a city attached.

**`Read Both Ad Blocks`** reads `top_ads` *and* `bottom_ads`, since a query often fills only one, and takes the advertiser from the display URL - the `link` is frequently a Google click tracker.

**`Update The Roster Maths`** compares the sweep against a Data Table roster: sweeps seen, first seen, whether the headline changed. Only advertisers that are new, rewritten or newly missing reach GPT-5.6, which reads the creative and says what they are doing.

**`Route By Lane`** splits three ways. Copy naming your brand pages the channel; a rival on your keyword goes in a digest with anyone who has stopped; everything familiar stays quiet.

### Setup

1. Bright Data: a SERP zone as one Header Auth credential. Free tier is 5,000 credits a month, no card.

2. An OpenAI credential and a Slack credential.

3. A Data Table called `brand_bidding` with columns `watch_key`, `advertiser`, `query`, `country`, `location`, `first_seen`, `last_seen`, `sweeps_seen`, `misses` and `last_headline`.

4. A sheet with a `sightings` tab, pasted into **`Log Every Sighting`**.

5. In **Settings**: your brand, the domains you own, any authorised resellers, and markets as `country=City,Region,Country`, separated by `|`.

## 1. The same grid every morning
Your brand crossed with the modifiers people actually type, in the countries you sell in. Fixed on purpose: a grid that varies makes yesterday's absence unreadable.

## 2. Read both ad blocks, not just the top one
Measured live: `hubspot alternative` filled `top_ads` and left `bottom_ads` empty, `asana alternative` did the opposite. Reading one field reports a clean sweep.

## 3. Who was here yesterday
The table is read, not filtered against. Every cell is swept every run; the history only decides what is worth saying about it.

## 4. Log everything, read what changed
The Filter drops the marker row that keeps a quiet morning alive, so it never reaches the sheet. Only new, rewritten or newly gone advertisers cost a token.

## 5. What is the advertiser actually doing
The model reads the creative and says whether it is a comparison, an imitation, a reseller or a coincidence. Whether it names you is a string test, decided in code.

## 6. Three different amounts of your attention
Your name in someone's ad copy is a trademark question. A rival on your keyword is competition. Everything familiar is neither.

## 7. One message per lane
Built in code and posted once. A Slack node fed twelve items posts twelve times, which is how a finding becomes something people mute.

## An ad above your brand is not automatically illegal

In most of the world a competitor may bid on your brand name as a keyword. What is usually restricted is using it *in the ad text* - and even that has exceptions for resellers, comparison sites, affiliates and honest referential use. This workflow can tell you which of those is happening on the wording; it cannot tell you whether you have a case.

So the escalation lane is a lane, not a verdict. Read the ad yourself before you file anything with Google or with a lawyer, and check that the advertiser is not a partner somebody else in your company signed.

**A sweep is a sample.** Google runs an auction per query, and the same query returned zero ads on one call and four on the next while this was being built. That is why nothing is reported as gone until it has missed `gone_after` sweeps in a row, and why a one-city grid will read quieter than the market really is.

**A market is a city, not a country.** The ads you see depend on where Google thinks the searcher is, so each market carries a city and the sweep reports that city - not your whole country. Add a second city rather than assuming the first one speaks for the market.

Each grid cell is one Bright Data request per run. Six modifiers across two markets is 12 requests a day, about 360 a month. Raise `max_queries` only when you have seen what one morning costs.
